title: Ombuds
pitch: A form that teaches the agent how to fill it, refuses the answers it cannot accept, corrects the agent when it is wrong, and hands every value to a human before it counts.
about_excerpt: A form that teaches the agent how to fill it, refuses the answers it cannot accept, corrects the agent when it is wrong, and hands every value to a human before it counts. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Ombuds is a work authorization worksheet, rebuilt so that the page is the authority instead of the agent. The worst forms on the web are long conditional government forms. A work authorization application asks you for an eligibility category code, and that one answer silently rewrites which of the next forty questions apply to you. Pick category c(3)(C) and you now owe a CIP code and an employer E-Verify number. Pick c(9) and neither of those exists, and you owe an I-485 receipt number instead. Say you want a Social Security card and both your parents' names become mandatory. None of this is written down anywhere the form can show you. It lives in footnotes and in the head of whoever has filled one out before. Agents are bad at these forms for the same reason people are. An agent reading the screen has no way to know that picking a category changed the rules. A backend MCP server cannot help either, because it has no idea what the person sitting in the browser has already answered. Ombuds moves the rules into the page and hands them to the agent directly. You talk to your agent in plain language about your situation. The page tells the agent exactly which questions apply to you right now, gives it the precise list of values each answer accepts, rejects anything malformed with the actual rule and a valid example so the agent fixes itself, and then holds every single value in a review queue until you personally accept it. Nothing an agent says about your immigration status is true until you agree with it. Three things it deliberately will not do. It will not tick your certification, because only the person filing can attest to their own application, so there is no tool for it at all. It will not give legal consent on your behalf, so the field authorizing disclosure to the Social Security Administration refuses agent writes outright. It will not let you generate your filing packet until every section is valid, your review queue is empty, and you have signed by hand. It is an independent worksheet. It is not affiliated with USCIS, it does not file anything, and everything stays in the browser tab. Inspiration I spent a year doing missionary work in Cambodia and watched people lose months to paperwork written as though the rules were obvious. The rules are never obvious. Putting them in the page, where an agent can be told them directly and a person can still overrule the answer, is a better use of this standard than making a shopping cart marginally faster. How I used WebMCP Eight mechanics. The first five are things WebMCP can do that a backend integration structurally cannot. 1. The tool schemas are generated from live form state. answer-category-questions is one tool with one name. Its schema is assembled from whichever eligibility category you picked. Category c(9) advertises a single field. Category c(3)(C) advertises four completely different ones. Change your category and the tool is unregistered and registered again with an entirely different shape. A server-side tool would have to accept a vague bag of optional strings and hope for the best. This one accepts exactly the four things you actually owe and rejects anything else as FIELD_NOT_APPLICABLE. Every enum is generated the same way from the same lists the HTML renders, so an agent cannot invent a state code or a category code, because the accepted values are sitting in the schema it was handed. 2. One predicate drives both the human UI and the agent's schema. Every conditional field carries a single showWhen function. The renderer uses it to decide whether to draw an input. The WebMCP layer uses the same one to decide whether that field belongs in the tool's schema. The human and the agent are looking at the same form, always, because there is only one description of the form and it cannot drift out of step with itself. 3. Tools appear and disappear so the agent only ever sees a legal move. Sections unlock as their prerequisites become valid, and a section's tool exists only while that section is open. Before Part 1 is valid there is no set-personal-info to call. Answer no to having used other names and add-other-name is not disabled, it is gone. Say your mailing address is where you live and set-physical-address unregisters itself. The agent gets a state machine rather than a flat API, and toolchange tells it when the machine moved. The sidebar shows the live registered set so you can watch tools flash in and out as you answer. 4. Rejections are structured, so the agent corrects itself. The page owns the validation rules, so it can hand back something an agent can act on instead of a red border. Send a bad SEVIS number and you get a machine-readable code, the rule in plain language, where to find the real value on your Form I-20, and a concrete valid example. The agent reads that and fixes its own argument on the next call. Nobody retypes anything. Cross-field conflicts work the same way. Claim category c(3)(C) while declaring H-1B status and you get the specific contradiction with both responsible fields named, because that is the class of error that actually gets real filings bounced back weeks later. 5. Nothing an agent writes is true until a human agrees. State is kept in two layers. Committed values are what the applicant accepted. Pending values are what the agent proposed. Proposals are validated the instant they arrive so the agent gets its feedback immediately without waiting on a human, and they surface in the page as amber diff cards with accept and reject buttons. Only a human click promotes a value. 6. Both halves of the spec, each where it fits. The imperative API carries the conditional sections, because branching logic is exactly what a form cannot express. The category finder at the top of the page is a declarative <form> carrying toolname , tooldescription and toolparamdescription , which a supporting browser turns into a tool with no registerTool call at all, and its submit handler answers the agent through SubmitEvent#respondWith() so the page never navigates away and throws out the conversation. Declarative suits that panel because it is a flat search over a fixed list. One ranked search with synonym expansion backs both paths, so a person typing "spouse of an H-1B worker" and an agent sending the same words get the same answer. Using each API where it fits is the argument the WebMCP explainer itself makes, and building both is what made me believe it. The tag beside the finder reports whether the browser actually synthesized the declarative tool rather than inferring it from a version number, and declarative calls are badged separately in the call log. 7. Then one question whether I can file today or not. Answering that takes this form's rules, a filing window off my I-20, a fee and the documents I hold. That That expired document is not from this page at all. It is a vault on a different origin publishing tools to this one form and nothing else. So that the form asks what I hold and never receives it. Now it asked me to sign and its tool call is suspended right this second waiting on a human being. This is still an open question in the specific specification. It can ask for a signature. It cannot sign. Only my click resolves that call and that boundary is deliberate. So I spent a year in Cambodia watching people lose months to paperwork written as though the rules were obvious. They never are. And so this is a form and thing that I built that looks like when it stops pretending.

live_observation.first_impression: A work authorization worksheet presents guided controls, conditional form sections, a document vault, and an agent tool surface.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked Load sample to populate the worksheet with demo data.
live_observation.after_state: The sample action completed and the app remained on the worksheet, with the form and review/tool areas available for inspection.
live_observation.notes: The page explicitly warns that saving progress is off by default and exposes validation and human-review controls.
